items.content:
Every new idea in supply chain goes through the same stages.
Nobody cares.

Then people argue with it.

Then a few brave companies try it anyway.

Those companies get results.

And then people stop asking "does it work?" They start asking "why are my competitors doing it?"

One year into building Demand Driven MRP in the US and that's the shift I'm watching happen. It is not new to us as we saw the same shift happen in Europe, APAC, IMEA and LATAM.

We spent the first years explaining what DDMRP is. Then the conversation shifts to how companies are already using it.

Curiosity is replacing scepticism. And that's when markets start to move.

What's the last idea in your industry that went from "that won't work" to "why isn't everyone doing this"?

items.content:
She'd been a supply chain planner for 11 years.
Good at it. Really good. 

The kind who caught problems before the system did, knew every supplier quirk, and read a situation faster than anyone on the floor.

Last month she moved into marketing.

She told me she was tired of spending 70% of her week reacting to problems the system should have prevented.

"I used to love this job," she said. "Now I spend Monday firefighting last week's problems. Tuesday planning Friday's expedites. Wednesday justifying to procurement why I need stock we haven't forecast. By Friday I'm just hoping nothing explodes over the weekend."

She wasn't failing. Her system was doing exactly what it was designed to do.

MRP was built for a stable, predictable world. It optimises for efficiency in conditions that haven't existed for 20 years. Run it in a volatile environment and it amplifies every disturbance, turning small uncertainties into constant crises.

Here's what the numbers show:
→ 60-80% of a planner's week in a forecast-driven environment is reactive work
→ In a flow-based environment: under 20%

Same intelligence. Same experience. Different system.

She didn't burn out. Her system burned her out.

What percentage of your planning team's week is spent planning versus reacting?

Last week, on stage at SAPICS 2026, Cape Town SA.
I said something that didn’t land well with everyone in the room.

“AI won’t fix broken planning.”

Silence. Then nods. Then the good kind of uncomfortable.

Here’s the talk in three moves.

One. The way most companies plan today is broken. Forecast-driven, MRP logic from the 70s, dressed up in new dashboards. Same fragility, prettier reports.

Two. Bolt AI on top of that? You don’t get better decisions. You get the wrong decisions, faster. Garbage in, algorithm out.

Three. Competitiveness doesn’t come back from a smarter forecast. It comes back from flow. Buffers that absorb variability. Decoupling points that protect your lead times. Execution built on today’s reality, not last quarter’s spreadsheet.

Three steps. One direction: back to the roots.

I started posting on LinkedIn at 22 with zero clients and zero proof. The only useful thing I owned was a feed full of people already doing what I wanted.

So I started showing up in their comments, and eventually in their DMs.

Some of those DMs turned into calls. Some of those calls turned into meeting in person at a conference two years later. A few of them I now work with, travel with, or build products with.

I never stopped doing that. It's still part of my week now, with a bigger business and a lot less free time than I had at 22.

By the time I got fired, I still didn't have clients. What I had was a small group of people who knew my name and knew what I could do.

That group is the reason I have a business now.

Distinctiva exists because of conversations that started as a comment on someone else's post. Every client, every speaking slot, every partnership traces back to a specific person I decided to talk to first.

The ones from this year came the same way the ones from year one did.

Your ceiling has a lot to do with who you're standing next to.

Most people are standing alone on purpose, because sending the first message feels uncomfortable for about ten seconds and then never does again.

Which is why I said yes to the Kleo Mastermind.

I'm speaking in London on August 8, alongside Lara Acosta, Jake Ward and Cam Trew. Three of the people in these photos, which isn't an accident.

You'll get the sessions. You'll also spend a full day next to founders and operators who can change what your next year looks like, and that part never shows up on the agenda.

Every seat is vetted, so it stays a small room.

"Use storytelling"
"Just be consistent and comment 300 times"
"Why aren't we going viral yet, we've posted 3 times."

What's actually behind an account that drives real pipeline:

Positioning. ICP research. Profile optimization. Keyword strategy. Content buckets. Hook writing. Storytelling from real experience. Batch creation. Posting cadence. A daily comment routine. Power lists. Early commenting for visibility. Warm DMs. Repurposing frameworks. Call transcript mining. Newsletter strategy. AI search visibility. Design. Video. Analytics. Flywheel thinking...

All of this running at the same time.

All connected. All intentional.

Most people skip straight to "what should I post" without ever answering "who am I talking to, what do I want them to think, and what do I want them to do next."

LinkedIn isn't hard because content people love complexity.

It's hard because building something that compounds takes an actual system.

The accounts getting consistent inbound aren't posting more than everyone else.

They just stopped guessing and started running an engine.

And the difference shows up in the pipeline.

You don't build all of this at once, you build it in order.

items.content:
I outranked my country's vice president.

I was getting tagged over the week and went to see what it was. 

A ranking of the strongest Colombians on LinkedIn. 

I was at number 5.

Number 9 on the same list was the vice president. 

I don't think the vice president knows he lost to a girl who posts on the internet for a living (or even cares lol).

The rest of the names around me run the country:

→ the co-founder of Rappi
→ the president of Asobancaria
→ the CEO of BBVA Colombia
→ the presidents of Bavaria and Postobón

These are people running banks and companies worth billions. 

I have real respect for every name on that list.

And then there's me, a content strategist.

If you'd told the version of me sitting in a Colombian university lecture, studying these exact companies for class, that I'd end up on a list next to their founders and CEOs, I would have told you that's insane.

I laughed for a good minute. 

Then I got serious about what it shows.

Ten years ago, someone like me had no way to reach an audience this size. You needed a company behind you, a title, a budget, someone important to open the door.

Now the door is a phone and a point of view. That's the whole shift.

This is why I get so happy watching more Colombians do the same thing. The talent here was always here. Getting seen used to be the hard part, and being online changed that.

A personal brand puts you next to people with far more power, money, and history than you have. It brings the clients, the speaking invites, and the opportunities straight to you, without asking anyone for permission first.

You don't need to be from the right city or the right last name anymore. 

You need a point of view and the patience to keep posting.

PS: If you're building your presence from a place people tend to underestimate, I want to know where you're posting from.

I run my entire business from a 14-inch laptop.

My small screen opened up a big world.

This year alone I've been flown out to Serbia, a mastermind in Guangzhou, China, and a conference in Amsterdam. End of the month, London, for something exciting with the Kleo team.

My team is spread across 4 countries. Most of them are friends from school, university, or family. Remote since day 1. And the business has tripled while I've been on the road this year.

And none of it would exist without the same technology we all complain about.

We all love to complain about this new reality. Phones glued to our hands, brains fried by notifications, can't sit through a meal without checking something.

But sometimes I forget how insane it is that this is even possible.

20 years ago, a girl from Medellín, Colombia with no network, no money, and no connections in the rooms that matter would have been stuck. You either knew the right people or you didn't.

Today you can land in a country where you know nobody, open your laptop, post on LinkedIn, and 6 months later be on stage at a conference on the other side of the world.

I don't think we're grateful enough for how insane this is.

The internet is the most level playing field that's ever existed. Your zip code doesn't decide your ceiling anymore. Your content does.

If you've been sitting on the idea of starting, posting, building something online, this is your sign. The window has never been more open.

I'm building a community of people doing exactly this inside The LinkedIn Engine → https://lnkd.in/ecb5awAT

PS: yes, my screen is orange. It's flux, a blue light filter app. 10/10 recommend for better sleep.

Booking, payment, and prep for my consulting calls, I wanted all of it in one place.

On a custom site that actually looks like mine.

Right now the booking sits in one place, the $500 runs through a payment link, and the prep questions go out over email.

So I opened Emergent and described exactly what I wanted:

- Pick a time
- Enter your details
- Answer 4 prep questions
- Pay the $500 fee
- Everything lands in one dashboard I can see

I turned that into one detailed prompt, dropped it in, and it built the whole thing. A real, working app, live just by typing into a chat.

I'm still going to play with it to get the brand colors and copy right. But HOW did it just build exactly what I asked for, right away?

I described what I wanted in plain English and had a working product back.

That still messes with my head.

Now it's one flow on a site that's actually mine. They pick a time, fill in their prep, pay, and it's all sitting there waiting for me before the call.

The way we work is moving fast. The repetitive, manual stuff that used to eat hours or live on a someday list is becoming stuff you can describe and have built for you.

For anyone who runs on systems (and yes, ADHD), building the thing in your head this easily is a different kind of freedom.

Whatever you've been putting off building, describe it to Emergent and see where it gets you.

items.content:
I spent my birthday in Medellín with people who drank ginger shots to make me feel loved. Nine hours, no alcohol, and the best conversations of my year.

They threw me a surprise party. 

No alcohol.
Ginger shots.
Cake with no sugar.
Vegetable and fruit mocktails. 

Some of my friends laugh, some of them love it, all of them stay.

That's the beauty of friendship. The people who love you will find a way to enjoy what you enjoy, even when it's not what they'd have picked. They planned the whole thing around it.

I don't need alcohol to have fun anymore. 

And trust me that took some unlearning.

Psychologists have a name for what drinking does in these settings: alcohol myopia. It narrows your attention until whatever is bothering you sits outside your field of view.

The problem is nothing gets fixed.

You just lose the capacity to hold it.

Most people drink to get through the room. The social anxiety doesn't leave, you just stop having the attention available to notice it, so it feels like it did.

Then you spend years assuming you can't walk into the room without it.

Sober, you keep all of it, and you find out you can still dance from 2pm to 11pm. Speak to strangers and actually be there, the real you.

No hangover. Real conversations with the actual versions of my friends, not the drunk ones.

Thanks to everyone here who sent me a message this weekend. I still can't explain what this app and the people on it have done for my life.

Back to work now.

Back to a week where we still make room for this. 

💚.
